For maintenance therapy, administer 250 mg orally at bedtime for six months or 300 mg orally twice daily. 3. For doses of 13-15 mg/kg/day, administer orally, divided every 6-12 hours, with food. 4. Ursodiol has orphan drug designation for the treatment of cystic fibrosis-associated liver disease and Niemann-Pick disease type C. 5. Post-Kasai procedure, administer ursodiol orally at 10-20 mg/kg/day, divided every 8-12 hours. 6. Aluminum hydroxide reduces the effects of ursodiol through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 7. Calcium carbonate reduces the effects of ursodiol through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 8. Crofelemer increases ursodiol levels through inhibition of transporters MRP2 and OATP1A2 in the gut. Systemic inhibition is unlikely due to minimal absorption. Use caution and monitor closely. 9. Eluxadoline increases ursodiol levels by decreasing its metabolism. It may also increase systemic exposure of co-administered OATP1B1 substrates. Use caution and monitor closely. 10. Ethinylestradiol reduces the effects of ursodiol through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 11. Cholestyramine reduces the effects of ursodiol through pharmacodynamic antagonism. The clinical significance is minor or unknown. 14. Monitor liver function tests (gamma-GT, alkaline phosphatase, AST, ALT) and bilirubin levels every three months for the first three months of therapy, and every six months thereafter. Discontinue therapy if parameters increase to clinically significant levels. 18. Ursodiol therapy may take several months to dissolve gallstones, and complete dissolution may not occur. Recurrence of gallstones may happen within five years in up to 50% of patients. 19. Ursodiol is naturally present in human milk. There are no reports of adverse effects on breastfed children, but data is limited. Consider the benefits of breastfeeding alongside the mother’s clinical need for therapy. 20. Ursodiol reduces cholesterol secretion from the liver and decreases fractional reabsorption of cholesterol in the intestines. 21. Ursodiol is rapidly taken up by the liver, conjugated with glycine or taurine, and excreted in bile. Nonabsorbed ursodiol is metabolized in the colon to lithocholic acid. 22. Ursodiol metabolites include glyco-ursodeoxycholic acid, tauro-ursodeoxycholic acid, and inactive compounds such as 7-keto-lithocholic acid and lithocholic acid. 23. Ursodiol is primarily excreted in feces. 24. Gallbladder stone dissolution with ursodiol is limited to radiolucent, non-calcified, high-cholesterol-content gallstones. 25. Use caution in patients with chronic liver disease, nonvisualizing gallbladders, or those requiring cholecystectomy. Discontinue therapy if gallbladder nonvisualization occurs during treatment. 26. Patients with variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, ascites, or requiring urgent liver transplantation should receive appropriate specific treatment. 27. Available data on ursodiol use in pregnancy, derived from randomized controlled trials and observational studies, do not indicate a drug-associated risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. Most exposures occurred in the second and third trimesters. 28. Ursodiol has a bioavailability of 90%, with an initial response for gallstone dissolution observed within 3-6 months. Approximately 70% of the drug is protein-bound. 29. Adding plans allows comparison of formulary status with other drugs in the same class.
